new.title: Find Louis XV dressed as a Roman emperor on Place Royale
new.desc: This classical square was laid out from 1758 to a plan by Jean-Gabriel Legendre, with a monument to Louis XV by Jean-Baptiste Pigalle unveiled in 1765. Revolutionaries pulled the king down in 1792, and the bronze you see now, by Pierre Cartellier, went up in 1819, while Pigalle's allegorical figures on the pedestal survived.
new.tip: Look for the seated figure of a contented citizen on the pedestal, said to be Pigalle's self-portrait. The square is a two-minute walk from the cathedral, so cross it on the way to the shops.
new.q: Place Royale, Reims

new.title: Read the champagne story in mosaics on Le Cellier
new.desc: Built in 1896 as a champagne trading house and long known locally as the Jacquart cellars, Le Cellier has a facade decorated with mosaic panels showing the stages of champagne making. The city bought it in 2010 and reopened it in 2015 as a cultural centre with exhibition space, performance halls and workshops.
new.tip: Check the programme for exhibitions and workshops inside, then admire the facade from across the street. It sits on Rue de Mars, a short walk from the Halles du Boulingrin.
new.q: Le Cellier, 4 Rue de Mars, Reims

new.title: See a president's DS at the Reims automobile museum
new.desc: Founded in 1985 around the collection of car designer Philippe Charbonneaux, this museum on Avenue Georges Clemenceau shows around 230 cars and motorbikes, one of the largest vehicle collections in France. Highlights include a 1962 Citroën DS used as President Giscard d'Estaing's official car and a Delage with a Lalique mascot, plus thousands of miniatures and pedal cars.
new.tip: A good rainy-day plan with children, who love the pedal cars. Opening hours vary by season and it is closed on Tuesdays, so check before you go.
new.q: Musée de l'Automobile, 84 Avenue Georges Clemenceau, Reims

new.title: Visit the crypt of 2,000 relics at Sainte-Clotilde
new.desc: This neo-Romanesque basilica in the south of Reims was built from 1896 to 1905 for the 1,400th anniversary of the baptism of Clovis, and named after his wife Clotilde. Cardinal Langénieux asked dioceses all over France for relics of saints who shaped the nation, and the crypt now holds more than 120 reliquaries and over 2,000 relics.
new.tip: It is in a residential district well off the tourist trail, so combine it with the Saint-Remi quarter about 15 minutes' walk north.
new.q: Basilique Sainte-Clotilde, Reims

new.title: Dine at Les Crayères, Madame Pommery's former mansion
new.desc: Le Parc, the restaurant of the Domaine Les Crayères, occupies an early 20th-century château that once belonged to the Pommery family, set in landscaped grounds on Boulevard Henry Vasnier. Chef Christophe Moret holds two Michelin stars here, confirmed in the 2026 guide.
new.tip: Dress up a little and book well ahead. Come for lunch to see the park in daylight, and walk off dessert among the Pommery and Ruinart estates next door.
new.q: Domaine Les Crayères, 64 Boulevard Henry Vasnier, Reims

new.title: Eat oysters behind the fishmonger's counter at Le Bocal
new.desc: Le Bocal is the small restaurant tucked behind the Poissonnerie des Halles, a fishmonger that has traded opposite the Boulingrin market for more than 20 years. The menu follows the catch and the seasons, with oysters, shellfish and simply cooked fish, and the champagne list is picked to match.
new.tip: It is closed on Sundays and Mondays and the room is small, so book. Lunch is the classic time to go, after a browse through the market.
new.q: Le Bocal, 27 Rue de Mars, Reims

new.title: Buy champagne-cork chocolates at Deléans
new.desc: Chocolaterie Deléans has been making sweets in Reims since 1874. Its signature is the bouchon de champagne, a chocolate shaped like a champagne cork and filled with marc de champagne, the local brandy, alongside bars and other classic Champagne specialities.
new.tip: The bouchons make an easy gift that survives a suitcase better than a bottle. The shop is on Rue Cérès, just north of Place Royale.
new.q: Deléans, 20 Rue Cérès, Reims

new.title: Have a glass in the open-air courtyard of Le Clos
new.desc: Le Clos is an open-air wine bar on Rue du Temple, steps from the Boulingrin market, with a long wine list and a courtyard terrace. By day it is a relaxed patio; after dark it turns into a lively bar with DJ sets and cocktails.
new.tip: It opens in the evening on weekdays and from midday on Saturday, and is usually closed on Sundays and Mondays. Come early on a warm evening to get a table outside.
new.q: Le Clos, 25 Rue du Temple, Reims

new.title: Travel back to the sky of 1789 at the Reims planetarium
new.desc: Opened in 1980 as the first planetarium in France outside Paris, it moved in 2013 into a new building on Rue du Général de Gaulle. Its shows trace the Moon, planets and constellations, and its projector can recreate the sky over Reims on any date in history.
new.tip: Book a session ahead in the school holidays, when shows for children fill up. It is a good stop on a grey day.
new.q: Planétarium, 49 Rue du Général de Gaulle, Reims

new.title: Cheer for the red and whites at the Stade Auguste-Delaune
new.desc: Stade de Reims, six times champions of France, played the first European Cup final in 1956 and lost again to Real Madrid in the 1959 final. Their home ground, opened in 1935 and rebuilt in 2008, holds about 20,500 fans and hosted matches of the 2019 Women's World Cup.
new.tip: Tickets are usually easy to get on match day except against the big clubs. The stadium is a 20-minute walk south of the centre along the Vesle.
new.q: Stade Auguste-Delaune, Reims

new.title: Catch a circus show in the 1867 ring of Le Manège
new.desc: City architect Narcisse Brunette designed a riding hall and a round circus building, modelled on the Cirque d'Été in Paris, which opened in 1867 beside the Patte d'Oie garden. Today they form Le Manège, the national stage of Reims, with a 475-seat theatre and an 800-seat circus programming contemporary circus, dance and theatre.
new.tip: Contemporary circus is the speciality, so pick a show in the round hall if you can. The Patte d'Oie park outside is nice for a stroll before curtain up.
new.q: Le Manège, 2 Boulevard du Général Leclerc, Reims

new.title: Tour Martel's chalk pits and old champagne tools
new.desc: On the Saint-Nicaise hill, the G.H. Martel house welcomes visitors into chalk quarries turned cellars, some of them medieval. Its 18th-century buildings hold an eco-museum of old regional tools and machines that show each stage of champagne making, and the visit ends with a tasting.
new.tip: It is a smaller, more relaxed alternative to the big houses nearby and usually good value. Book ahead, especially at weekends.
new.q: Champagne G.H. Martel, 17 Rue des Créneaux, Reims

new.title: Step inside the workers' palace of the Familistère de Guise
new.desc: Stove maker Jean-Baptiste André Godin, inspired by Fourier's utopian ideas, built this Social Palace for his workers between 1859 and 1884, with glass-roofed courtyards, a school, a theatre and a swimming pool. The workers' cooperative he set up ran the factory until 1968, and the site has been a museum since 2010.
new.tip: Allow half a day: there are restored flats, the theatre and the laundry with its pool to explore. Godin stoves were made here, so look for them around the museum.
new.q: Familistère, Guise

new.title: Look up at the lonely spires of Saint-Jean-des-Vignes
new.desc: Founded in 1076 on a hill above Soissons, this abbey was sacked by Huguenots in 1567 and its church sold after the Revolution, when most of the nave was pulled down. What remains is a soaring Gothic west front with two spires, built between 1488 and 1520, standing on its own like a stage set.
new.tip: The ruins belong to the town and can be visited freely in the warmer months. Stand at the far end of the lawn for the best photo of the facade.
new.q: Abbaye Saint-Jean-des-Vignes, Soissons

new.title: Look down on Givet from the Charlemont citadel
new.desc: Charles V ordered this fortress in 1554 on a cliff 80 metres above the Meuse, and after Givet became French in 1697 Vauban strengthened it further. The vast site now opens to visitors with views over the river and the Belgian border.
new.tip: Much of the site is free to roam, and only the eastern point is paid. It opens from April to early November; in mid-August a hot-air balloon festival takes off from the fort.
new.q: Fort de Charlemont, Givet

new.title: See the 'Voyelles' manuscript at the Rimbaud museum
new.desc: The Vieux Moulin, a ducal watermill built across the Meuse in 1626, has housed the Arthur Rimbaud museum since 1991. Over four floors it follows the poet from his Charleville childhood through Paris and Verlaine to Africa, showing only original documents, including his travel case and the manuscript of 'Voyelles'.
new.tip: The paper works rotate every six months to protect them from light, so a second visit can show you different manuscripts. The Place Ducale is a few minutes' walk away.
new.q: Musée Arthur Rimbaud, Quai Arthur Rimbaud, Charleville-Mézières

new.title: Learn champagne's history inside Château Perrier
new.desc: Charles Perrier, son of the founder of Perrier-Jouët, built this brick and stone château on the Avenue de Champagne between 1852 and 1857. Since May 2021 it has housed Épernay's museum of champagne wine and regional archaeology, covering everything from prehistoric finds to the making of champagne.
new.tip: It is the best place to get your bearings before a day of cellar visits on the avenue. Moët & Chandon and Mercier are within a few minutes' walk.
new.q: Château Perrier, 13 Avenue de Champagne, Épernay

new.title: Find the arrow slits in Plomion's fortified church
new.desc: In the Thiérache, 71 village churches were turned into brick strongholds between the 16th and 17th centuries to shelter villagers from passing armies. Plomion's is one of the most impressive, with a square keep flanked by two round towers and about 60 loopholes; it reopened in 2023 after a four-year restoration.
new.tip: Plan a loop by car to see several fortified churches in a day, such as Parfondeval and Burelles nearby. The Thiérache tourist office in Vervins has route maps.
new.q: Église Notre-Dame, Plomion

new.title: Lunch at Les Avisés, the Selosse family's table in Avize
new.desc: In a grand house in the Côte des Blancs village of Avize, the family behind the cult grower Champagne Jacques Selosse opened this hotel and restaurant in 2011. The cooking is French and seasonal, and the wine list runs deep in grower champagnes as well as other French regions.
new.tip: Booking is by phone or email rather than online, and the dining room is small, so reserve early. Walk off lunch in the chardonnay vineyards above the village.
new.q: Les Avisés, 59 Rue de Cramant, Avize

new.title: Buy cave-ripened maroilles at the Fontaine Orion farm
new.desc: In the green hedged pastures of the Thiérache, the Halleux family has made farmhouse maroilles from their own cows' raw milk since 1983. They are the last producers in the whole maroilles appellation to ripen their cheese in a natural cellar, and also make the tarragon-flavoured Dauphin and cream of maroilles.
new.tip: Buy a tarte au maroilles from the farm shop for a picnic. The shop closes on Sundays, and farm tours with tastings run on some summer days, so phone ahead.
new.q: Ferme de la Fontaine Orion, Rue d'Hurtebise, Haution

new.title: Taste a beer named for Rimbaud at the Brasserie d'Arthur
new.desc: This Charleville brewery makes the Cuvée d'Arthur, a range of Belgian-style beers named in homage to the poet Arthur Rimbaud, who was born in the town. Its production site welcomes visitors for tours and tastings, and the shop sells the full range.
new.tip: Pair a tasting with a platter of Ardennes charcuterie. Tours are in French and hours vary, so call ahead.
new.q: Brasserie d'Arthur, Rue Jean-Baptiste Lefort, Charleville-Mézières

new.title: Eat wood-fire grills at La Grillade Gourmande in Épernay
new.desc: A short walk from the Avenue de Champagne, this restaurant cooks over a wood fire: whole sea bass with fennel, rib of beef, Iberian pork and game in season. It has a garden terrace that is lovely in summer and is listed in the Michelin Guide.
new.tip: It is closed on Sundays and Mondays. A good counterpoint to a day of tastings, as the menu leans hearty.
new.q: La Grillade Gourmande, 16 Rue de Reims, Épernay

new.title: Treat yourself at Jérôme Feck in Châlons
new.desc: In the Hôtel d'Angleterre in the centre of Châlons-en-Champagne, chef Jérôme Feck holds a Michelin star, confirmed in 2026, for modern cooking known for its intense, balanced sauces. Next door, his bistro Les Temps Changent serves more traditional dishes at gentler prices.
new.tip: It is closed on Sundays and Mondays and books by phone. Combine it with an evening canal boat trip in summer.
new.q: Jérôme Feck, 19 Place Monseigneur Tissier, Châlons-en-Champagne

new.title: Dine classic French at Le Grand Cerf below the Montagne de Reims
new.desc: This imposing inn on the road from Reims to Épernay sits at the foot of the Montagne de Reims, with a garden and terrace. Chef Dominique Giraudeau, long at Les Crayères under Gérard Boyer, cooks classic French dishes with lobster, game and truffles, and holds a Michelin star.
new.tip: It is closed on Tuesdays and Wednesdays and serves only lunch on Sundays. Afterwards, drive up through the forest to the Faux de Verzy.
new.q: Le Grand Cerf, 50 Route Nationale, Montchenot

new.title: Explore the tunnels under Laon's hilltop
new.desc: The 'Secrets sous la ville' tour takes you into the underground galleries hollowed out beneath the upper town of Laon, with an audio guide that tells the city's story from its geology onwards. It stays at a steady 11°C all year.
new.tip: Tickets and audio guides are collected at the tourist office on the cathedral square, 30 minutes before departure, with ID; the entrance is about 550 metres away. Bring a jumper.
new.q: Office de tourisme, Place du Parvis Gautier de Mortagne, Laon

new.title: Hike to the Dames de Meuse cliffs above the river
new.desc: Near Laifour, three great wooded ridges of rock rise to about 400 metres above a tight bend of the Meuse. Legend says they are three unfaithful wives turned to stone on the day their crusader husbands took Jerusalem. The site has been protected since 1997.
new.tip: The trails from Laifour climb steeply to viewpoints over the river loop, so wear proper shoes. Laifour has a station on the Charleville to Givet line.
new.q: Les Dames de Meuse, Laifour

new.title: Watch eagles fly over Château-Thierry's castle walls
new.desc: Inside the ruins of the medieval castle above Château-Thierry, the falconers of Les Aigles de Château-Thierry fly eagles, owls, falcons and ravens in educational shows. The castle hill also gives a broad view over the Marne valley and its vineyards.
new.tip: Shows are usually at 3 pm and 5 pm from Tuesday to Sunday during the season, roughly March to November. Arrive early for a seat with a view.
new.q: Château médiéval, Château-Thierry

new.title: Go underground in the Nichet caves near Givet
new.desc: Near the Belgian border at Fromelennes, the Nichet caves have welcomed visitors since the 1890s and reopened with electric lighting in 1987. Guided tours lead about 35 metres underground through limestone halls hung with stalactites, with light and sound effects along the way.
new.tip: Open from spring to autumn, with longer hours in July and August. Combine it with the Charlemont citadel in Givet, ten minutes away.
new.q: Grottes de Nichet, Fromelennes

new.title: Tour the Launois wine museum in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger
new.desc: The Launois family, growers since 1872, has assembled a large museum of old presses, tools and machines in its house in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, one of the grand cru villages of the Côte des Blancs. A guided visit of about two hours leads through the collections and the chalk cellars and ends with a tasting.
new.tip: Visits start in the morning and should be booked ahead. Taste a blanc de blancs here, as Le Mesnil is pure chardonnay country.
new.q: Champagne Launois, 2 Avenue Eugène Guillaume, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger

new.title: Paddle or walk the shores of the Lac des Vieilles Forges
new.desc: Created by a dam in 1927 in the forest north-west of Charleville, this 150-hectare lake is about 3.5 km long with some 12 km of wooded shoreline. Motorboats are banned, leaving it to sailors, canoeists, rowers and anglers, and there is a beach and a forest adventure park.
new.tip: Follow the path around the lake for an easy half-day walk. In July the lake hosts an open-water swimming race, a sign of how popular it is in summer.
new.q: Lac des Vieilles Forges, Les Mazures
